segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then I heard a loud voice from the temple saying to the seven angels,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Go and pour out the seven bowls of the fury of God onto the earth.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So the first went and poured out his bowl onto the earth, and a foul and malignant sore came upon the people who had the mark of the beast and who worshipped its image.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The second poured out his bowl into the sea, and it became blood like that of a corpse, and every living creature died, everything in the sea.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The third poured out his bowl into the rivers and the springs of water, and they became blood.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And I heard the angel of the waters saying,

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: “You are just, you who are and who were, the Holy One, because you have given these judgments,

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: for they poured out the blood of holy ones and prophets, and you have given them blood to drink. They deserve it.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And I heard the altar saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Yes, Lord God, the Almighty, true and just are your judgments.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The fourth poured out his bowl on the sun, and it was allowed to scorch people with fire.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: People were scorched with a fierce heat, and they blasphemed the name of God, who has authority over these plagues, and they did not turn back to give him glory.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The fifth poured out his bowl on the throne of the beast, and its kingdom was plunged into darkness. People gnawed their tongues from the pain,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and they blasphemed the God of heaven because of their pains and their sores, and they did not turn back from their deeds.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The sixth poured out his bowl on the great river Euphrates, and its water was dried up, so that the way might be prepared for the kings from the rising of the sun.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And I saw three unclean spirits like frogs coming out of the mouth of the dragon, out of the mouth of the beast and out of the mouth of the false prophet.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For they are spirits of demons performing signs, which go out to the kings of the whole inhabited world to gather them for the battle of the great day of God the Almighty.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Look, I am coming like a thief. Blessed is the one who stays awake and keeps his clothes on, so that he will not walk about naked and have people see his shame.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And they gathered them to the place that is called in Hebrew Harmagedon.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The seventh poured out his bowl on the air, and a loud voice came out of the temple, from the throne, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “It is done!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And there were flashes of lightning, rumblings and peals of thunder, and there was a great earthquake, such as there had never been since people came to be on the earth, so mighty an earthquake, so great.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The great city split into three parts, and the cities of the nations fell. And Babylon the great was remembered before God, to give her the cup of the wine of the fury of his wrath.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Every island fled, and no mountains were to be found.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And huge hailstones, each weighing about a talent, came down from the sky on people, and people blasphemed God because of the plague of the hail, for that plague was exceedingly great.

notes.phrase: a loud voice from the temple
notes.note: The speaker is not identified. Because the previous verse (15:8) says no one could enter the temple until the plagues were finished, many interpreters take the voice to be God's own, as also the voice from the throne in verse 17. The text leaves it unnamed, and the translation does the same.

Most translations render this word 'wrath' here. Verse 19 uses it side by side with a second Greek word for anger (orgē), and translations then need two English words. This translation uses 'fury' for the first and 'wrath' for the second throughout the chapter, so the reader can see that the bowls of verse 1 and the cup of verse 19 share the same term.

Greek has a single word-family where English has two: 'righteous' and 'just', 'righteousness' and 'justice'. Here and in verse 7 the subject is God's judging, so 'just' is used. Older versions have 'righteous' in both places.

The King James Version reads 'which art, and wast, and shalt be', following an edition of the Greek text that rested here on a scholarly conjecture, not on manuscripts. The manuscripts read 'the Holy One', and all modern editions follow them. The Greek word is different from the one behind 'holy ones' in verse 6. It describes one who is devout or faithful, and in the Septuagint is used of God as well as of his loyal people.

The traditional rendering is 'saints', which now suggests canonised individuals or people of unusual virtue. The word is used of all members of the community as people set apart for God. Many translations keep 'saints', and others use 'God's people' or 'his holy people'.

The traditional rendering is 'repent', which in modern English centres on feeling sorry. The Greek word carries the prophets' call to return to God, a change of direction in mind and conduct. Most translations keep 'repent' as an established term understood to include a change of life.

The Euphrates was the eastern frontier of the Roman world, and beyond it lay the Parthian empire, Rome's most feared rival. For a first-century reader, a dried-up Euphrates meant the border standing open to invasion from the east. The image also recalls the drying of the Red Sea and the Jordan, and the prophets' oracles about the fall of Babylon, which stood on this river.

notes.phrase: “Look, I am coming like a thief.
notes.note: The narrative is interrupted by a voice speaking in the first person. No speaker is named, but the words match what the risen Jesus says to the churches earlier in the book (3:3 on coming like a thief, 3:18 on clothing and the shame of nakedness), and the saying is generally taken as his. The description of the kings being gathered resumes in verse 16.

The familiar spelling 'Armageddon' comes from a different manuscript tradition. It has also become an English word for a world-ending catastrophe, whereas here it is a place name. The form printed follows the Greek text being translated. It is usually explained as Hebrew for 'mountain of Megiddo', a city on a plain where famous Old Testament battles were fought. No mountain of that name is known, and the derivation is disputed.

It is disputed which city is meant. Many take it to be Babylon, named in the next sentence and called 'the great city' later in the book. Others take it to be Jerusalem, which is called 'the great city' at 11:8 and would then be distinguished from 'the cities of the nations'. The translation leaves the phrase as open as the Greek.

notes.traditional: about a hundred pounds; the weight of a talent
notes.note: A talent was the largest common unit of weight. Its value varied with place and period, but estimates generally fall somewhere between about 25 and 40 kilograms (roughly 60 to 90 pounds). The point is hailstones of impossible size, far beyond anything in the Exodus plague of hail that the scene recalls.

candidates.reason: It recurs through Revelation and Paul alongside ὀργή, sometimes in the same phrase, so the two need fixed and distinct English renderings ('fury' and 'wrath' here).
Translators split between 'temple' and 'sanctuary', and the word needs distinguishing from ἱερόν (the whole temple complex) consistently across the Gospels, Paul and Revelation.
Translations vary between 'blaspheme', 'curse', 'slander' and 'revile' depending on whether the object is God or people, and a rule for the split is needed.
The word covers both physical prostration and worship, and translations vary between 'worship', 'bow down' and 'pay homage', especially in the Gospels and Revelation.
Rendering it 'holy' collides with the register's ἅγιος; a decision is needed on whether to distinguish it (e.g. 'devout', 'faithful') across Acts, the Pastorals, Hebrews and Revelation.
